title: Iran-Linked Water Hack Probe Widens as Japan Bets $60B on AI Compute
subhead: US investigators examine whether Iranian hackers hit water utilities across at least seven states, while Japan maps a $60 billion AI data-center buildout and Europe's AI ambitions collide with its Huawei ban.

sections.heading: US water-system cyber incidents widen, attribution contested
sections.body:
The FBI said at least seven states reported cyber activity affecting water utilities last week, forcing some systems to switch to manual operations, according to CBS News and Yahoo News. Investigators are examining whether Iranian hackers were responsible, per US officials cited by CBS.

Republican Rep. Mike Turner, who previously chaired the House Intelligence Committee, told CBS's Face the Nation that critical infrastructure 'needs to be hardened' and that Congress had not been briefed on the incidents. He said adversaries including Russia, China, North Korea and Iran treat civilian-support infrastructure as 'valid military targets.'

Attribution is disputed at the top: President Trump said he did not believe Iranians were behind the activity and instead blamed Minnesota's state leadership, without providing evidence, according to the same report. The divergence between the FBI's investigation and the president's public stance is itself a data point about how quickly such incidents become politically contested.
sections.whyItMatters: Water utilities are low-friction targets with outdated industrial controls. A multi-state incident that cannot be cleanly attributed shows how ambiguity itself becomes leverage — deterrence is hard when no one agrees who did it.

sections.heading: Japan plans ~$60B AI data-center buildout
sections.body:
A Nikkei survey of 26 major Japanese data-center operators found that 22 plan to more than quadruple AI-focused capacity by 2033 versus end-2025 levels, at a combined cost of roughly 10 trillion yen (~$60 billion), according to Cryptobriefing's summary of the survey.

NTT leads domestically, targeting total capacity of 2 GW by fiscal 2033 and earmarking about 1.5 trillion yen (~$9–10 billion) toward building 1 GW of that. The report notes Blackstone, Microsoft and Mubadala are adding tens of billions more to the sector.

Comparable national programs are moving in parallel: the UK's AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, has called for tripling data-center capacity to 14 GW by 2030, and Nvidia has formally grouped eight Australian operators into a single 'sovereign AI' program.
sections.whyItMatters: The AI buildout is shifting from private hyperscaler capex to state-organized national programs. Computing capacity is being treated as strategic infrastructure — planned, sited and subsidized like power grids.

sections.heading: Berlin and Madrid resist an EU-wide Huawei ban — citing AI costs
sections.body:
Germany and Spain are leading opposition inside the European Council to the European Commission's draft plan to ban Huawei and ZTE equipment from EU telecom networks at bloc level, according to The Next Web. Both want high-risk-vendor decisions to stay at national level and warn an EU-wide ban would invite Chinese retaliation and inflate the cost of the AI-infrastructure buildout.

The detail explains Berlin's position: Huawei gear was still installed in roughly 60% of German 5G radio sites as recently as late 2024, and Germany's own phase-out plan requires core removal by end-2026 and broader radio-access removal by end-2029.

Spain's exposure differs: Telefónica renewed its 5G core contract with Huawei in late 2024 to run to 2030, and Spain entrusted significant fibre infrastructure to Huawei in summer 2025 — a decision the Commission flagged as creating dependence on a high-risk supplier in a sensitive sector.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe's security consensus is fracturing along cost lines. The AI buildout requires telecom upgrades at a scale the bloc hasn't budgeted for, so the same governments pushing sovereign compute are also pushing back on paying to remove Chinese gear.

sections.heading: Smuggling case details underscore enforcement gaps
sections.body:
Newly unsealed charging documents add detail to last week's arrest of a California tech CEO. Greg Lui, owner of Earthmade Computer Inc, is accused of arranging the illegal export of more than $300 million in export-controlled technology to China between 2023 and 2024, per Export Compliance Daily and Ars Technica.

Per the indictment, Lui shipped servers containing Nvidia A100, H100, RTX 4090 and RTX 5090 chips from three US manufacturers through Malaysia and Singapore, which did not require licenses, before onward re-export to China. Earthmade allegedly received more than $176 million from two Malaysian shipment companies between January and October 2024. Prosecutors said the activity continued as recently as August 2026. He faces up to 20 years on the export-control conspiracy count.
sections.whyItMatters: The case illustrates the mechanics of diversion: legal intermediate destinations plus falsified end-use paperwork. Controls set at the destination border are only as strong as the paperwork and freight-forwarder chain behind them.

sections.heading: Europe seeks a 'second strike' trade tool ahead of Beijing talks
sections.body:
EU trade chief Maroš Šefčovič will travel to Beijing on Thursday for two days of talks with Commerce Minister Wang Wentao aimed at averting a trade war, according to MSN reporting on the meetings. The backdrop is a record €360 billion Chinese trade surplus with the EU, per WAM.

Germany and France are pressing for a rapid-response 'second strike' market-cutoff tool to reduce supply-chain dependence, an issue The Economist ties directly to China's use of export controls on rare earths needed by defence-related firms. The talks come as a US-backed rare-earth supply chain rebuild continues to lag Chinese processing dominance.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe is trying to pair defensive trade instruments with a negotiating visit — leverage and dialogue in the same week. Whether member states accept a market-cutoff tool will determine if the EU can act as a single trade actor under pressure.

sections.heading: India's chip push comes with a warning about 'established interests'
sections.body:
India's IT minister Ashwini Vaishnaw told PTI that India's rise in semiconductor design and manufacturing would 'obviously' be seen as a threat by established players in the global chip value chain, and that the industry must prepare for cyberattacks and disruptions, according to the Economic Times.

It is a notable framing from a sitting minister: rather than presenting India's entry as purely commercial, Vaishnaw casts it as geopolitically contested terrain and says he has told the industry to stay vigilant.
sections.whyItMatters: As semiconductor supply chains diversify beyond East Asia, new entrants are treating their own factories and design capacity as targets. Industrial policy is converging with threat modelling.

sections.heading: AI compute moves toward orbit
sections.body:
Loft Orbital and UAE-based Marlan Space announced a $1 billion programme to expand an AI-equipped satellite constellation from 10 to 50 satellites, with Mistral supplying the on-board AI models, according to The Next Web. French President Emmanuel Macron announced it at the International Space Summit in Paris in September. Outlets described the financing differently — the firms call it a $1bn programme, Sifted reported a $1bn contract, and Bloomberg described a consortium-led $1bn investment.

Separately, India-based TakeMe2Space plans to launch MOI-1A, described as India's first orbital computing satellite, carrying Nvidia processors for AI inference, per Cryptobriefing.
sections.whyItMatters: Putting inference in orbit shifts compute away from terrestrial jurisdiction and power grids. It is an early signal that the compute-sovereignty contest may not stay on the ground.

bottomLine: Today's thread is the widening gap between stated strategy and delivery. The US is investigating multi-state water-utility intrusions it cannot confidently attribute, with the White House publicly disputing its own FBI's premise. Europe wants both a sovereign AI buildout and a bloc-wide Huawei ban, but Germany and Spain are working to keep the ban non-binding because the replacement cost competes with the AI spend. Japan, meanwhile, is moving to quadruple AI data-center capacity on a roughly $60 billion plan, and the chip-smuggling indictment shows how porous export controls remain in practice. The direction of travel — compute as national infrastructure, supply chains as contested terrain — is consistent; the execution is where the friction is.
sources: CBS News via Yahoo News, The Next Web, Cryptobriefing/Nikkei survey, Export Compliance Daily, Ars Technica, Reuters, MSN (EU-China talks), WAM via MSN, The Economist, Economic Times/PTI, Sifted, Bloomberg, Space Intel Report
